$comment: What makes a secret's name look like a key itself (SEC-033): the one source the gateway (tqa_types::is_key_shaped_name) and the web read, so the two can't diverge. A name is key-shaped when it starts with one of `prefixes` followed by a body of at least `length` characters: letters, digits, - or _ (`token`, the default) whose letters and digits, separators skipped, change class (digit, upper-case, lower-case) at at least `change_percent` % of their neighbouring places; or upper-case letters and digits only (`upper_digit`). Or when it holds a run of letters and digits (no - or _) matching one of `runs`: at least `length` long, with at least `classes` of the three classes, changing class at at least `change_percent` % of its neighbouring places. Random bodies change class often; readable names, CamelCase with a year included, rarely do. Kept conservative (the lead, 7 Oct): a refused real name is worse than a missed key, which the page's guard and log redaction still catch; so hf_token, or a prefix followed by words, is a name.
